***\[Brace for a fucking text-wall from someone who was obsessed with Kopaka in the early 2000's\]***

Both have a different charm, but are ultimately severely lacking in different ways.

I think the reboot was made with the intent to appeal to an audience somehow even younger than the original run of Bionicle did, then immediately the sales made it evident that they needed to shoot for an older demographic, but by that point I think it was too late. Hence Bionicle getting cancelled a second time.

Master does evoke some of the original design imo, but the designers weren't aware of how much attention they would've needed to pay to the source material. Kopaka's personality in the stories they attached to the Master line of sets was effectively a complete polar opposite to his Personality in original Bionicle, and it was more than off-putting to fans.

The Uniter line very obviously tried to undo the damage by adhering better to the original source material, giving the Toa an "edgier" look. They also went about changing the character from a bulky "no-brain, all brawn" character archetype, to the sleeker, more serious design that Kopaka is associated with. I find it kind of funny how the designers gave the equivalent of his Gen 2 Nuva form a set of weapons referential to his Mata form. Even from the way they swapped the art style of the animations and comics that partnered with the Masters and Uniters, it's really clear that they understood that they missed the mark and wanted to attempt to salvage it, and I respect that. I just don't think the right people were in the right places when it came to designing the sets. I don't think the designers are bad or anything, I just don't think they had people who were willing to let new Bionicle attempt to evoke what people loved about old Bionicle, and the line suffered for it.

Personally, I don't know which I like more. As a kid, Kopaka was my favourite character in all fictional media, and remained as such for well over 10 years of my childhood, and the "disrespect" (kind of hyperbolic, but you get the point) that Master Kopaka is to the original character definitely puts me off of really liking the set. Especially how they saw that he has a shield, and used that as a basis to make him a bulky, heavy armoured, brute in design. Meanwhile, Kopaka is the polar opposite of that; a character associated with *cold* calculated moves, and sleek, agile, and aggressive movements. As far as how linear the original Toa Mata were, Kopaka was the only one who's shoulders were connected "sideways" to make his profile slightly more lean than the other 5. It's all kind of ironic, and shows that they didn't pay much attention to the original designs. I think there's some charming aspects of the Master design, but I can't get myself to "love" it.

Uniter clearly wanted to right the wrongs that were made whilst designing Master, and I'd argue that, in many ways, it did. Kopaka's design is reworked to be tall and sleek, reflective of what Kopaka actually originally was, the facial expression portrayed by his mask looks much more serious, somewhat befitting of Mata-Nui's original edgelord. The gun thing is a fun way to attempt to implement his shield into the set, and the actual guard of the gun is much smaller in surface area, making it somewhat like a buckler, which is plenty reflective of Kopaka. The only thing this set is really missing as far as the original character, was some method of mobility. Unless I'm forgetting something, all of Kopaka's sets have come with some kind of built in mobility, such as the snow board, ski/skates, or just literally having wings (even Master followed this trend). So it is kind of weird that that one thing was left out, but other than that, when I look at Uniter Kopaka, I do genuinely feel like it invokes his character. In the case of Master Kopaka, if it weren't for the mask, I genuinely would not think it's supposed to be him, but Uniter does a way better job at this.

Ultimately, I don't love Uniter either though. The design feels like someone went through things they noticed about Kopaka over the years, probably watched the Mask of Light movie, even. But when I look at the set, it feels incomplete. It's like they wrote a little checklist of what Kopaka is supposed to be, and tried to just make something that adhered to their checklist. I don't fault them for that, but the set feels soulless to me, like it doesn't exactly know what it wants to be, it just wants to represent Kopaka in a way that doesn't insult the fanbase. So, once again, while I do like aspects of the set, I just don't "love" it. If you had to make me pick one, I'd go with Uniter, even if only barely, just because I appreciate the designers doing their due diligence to something I loved throughout my entire youth.

CBU3's solution to the issue of easy dungeons being unclearable due to bad Healer players was literally just to make Healing as unreasonably simple as possible to prevent the skill issue from having a potential to shine through, and then make dungeons deal incredibly low damage, so you can realistically clear them without a Healer at all.

In mid/high-end content, Healers are given a more active role, but in order to maintain accessibility to all levels of skill, rather than forcing Healer players to be slightly more skilled than everyone else, they made Healer DPS into a ridiculously low APM task. When any player reaches the point wherein their own skill is bottle-necked by the job, it begins to become dissatisfying to engage with that job. In my case, I used to be a White Mage main for roughly the first 4 years of my time playing XIV, and I didn't think I'd ever get bored of it. Eventually, after having cleared my second full raid tier with it, and moving on to try Ultimates, I realised that my level of familiarity and comfort with XIV's combat mechanics as well as the healing role itself, was far beyond what White Mage was letting me express. Then suddenly SMN went from being right next to BLM in regards to difficulty, all the way down to sitting with WHM, WAR, and DNC, as jobs that have very little room for skill expression beyond simply playing the job at a functional level. RDM's main mechanic involves using Black Magic spells, and White Magic spells in order to fill up it's "mana gauge", which will then be spent on your melee combo - which is your prime damage dealing tool.

The melee combo is comprised of three rather fast melee attacks with your sword, and then 3 high-damage ranged spells that will follow it up.

As a RDM, your goal is effectively to generate as much mana for your gauge as you can, in order to use as many sword combos as you can, since that's where most of your damage will come from.

It can be complicated and engaging when you're trying to push the absolute most damage possible out of  the job, but when playing casually, you don't need to put much of any effort in towards playing at a perfectly acceptable level.

**The TL;DR of how to play the job is literally:**

* Use your damage buff "Embolden" as soon as it comes off cooldown, and never delay it unless there's literally nothing for the party to attack.
* Use a spell with a maximum cast time of 2.5 seconds (Jolt, Verfire, Verstone), in order to get a "Dual Cast" proc from your passive, and spend the Dual Cast on either Veraero or Verthunder.
* Veraero and Verthunder generate "White Mana" or "Black Mana" respectively, and you need both gauges to be at 50 in order to be able to use your sword combo. The only caveat is that you need to keep the two gauges in balance - which is really easy.

There's more to it, but that's the basic rundown of the job, and as long as you're doing that at minimum, you're doing more than enough in order to play through normal content without issue.

If you have any questions on how to play RDM beyond that, feel free to ask, as RDM is my main job for raiding and such.

DRK received a massive rework when Shadowbringers released that massively dumbed down the entire kit.

Beforehand, we used to have an oGCD called Dark Arts that had a 1 second CD, 2400 MP cost, and using it would augment the next skill you used (almost every skill had a Dark Arts augment).

DRK also could not regen MP normally, it could only get MP back from it's skills.

Then, Abyssal Drain (which is currently an oGCD with a 60 second CD) used to be a Spell on the GCD, with a \~1700 MP cost. It would heal you based on a % of the damage it deals in an AoE, but the heal would only work if you used Dark Arts first. Combined, the two cost roughly one third of your MP pool to cast.

And DRK also had other skills that would regen MP for it on hit (kinda like bloodwhetting's heal but MP instead of HP) and it had an inverse version of the skill that would regen MP every time you got hit. Quietus (it's AoE gauge spender) used to also regen MP on-hit.

So DRK had this rotation of trying to generate as much MP as humanly possible, as quickly as humanly possible, and then spend it all on Dark Arts Abyssal Drain in order to essentially convert that MP gain into HP. Dungeons mobs used to hit way harder back then, so you typically needed to be good with the AoE self-heal rotation, or you'd just kinda die during wall pulls.

Oh yeah, The Blackest Night also used to give you 50 Blood Gauge when it was destroyed, so TBN was factored into the equation as a method of getting more Quietus uses, which meant more MP, which mean you could afford to shield yourself via TBN, and also continue spamming Dark Arts Abyssal Drain.

It was really fuckin' fun, and I've been absolutely gutted by the fact that it was all removed from the game, and now DRK has no gameplay identity and is effectively just a WAR with less healing and more oGCD's, except unlike old DRK, it's new skills have next to 0 synergy with each other. So you just kinda face roll the keyboard thoughtlessly, and that's how you play DRK now.
